fields.v: Neferu, M., Marian, C. V., Mitrea, D. A. (2026). Vibe Coding: A New Paradigm in Software Development Assisted by Artificial Intelligence. In: 2026 18th International Conference on Electronics, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (ECAI), pp. 1-8. IEEE. https://doi.org/10.1109/ECAI69016.2026.11613779
Conference — 2026 18th International Conference on Electronics, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (ECAI), IEEE, pp. 1-8, DOI 10.1109/ECAI69016.2026.11613779

National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest, Romania (Doctoral School, Faculty of Electronics, Telecommunications and IT; Faculty of Engineering in Foreign Languages) — academic

Evaluates; secondary: Proposes an approach — qualitative single case study: one developer builds a Task Manager web app with Claude only through prompts, times it against estimated classical development, audits security (OWASP ZAP) and code quality (ESLint); proposes a three-layer Minimum Viability Framework for vibe-coded applications and a conceptual distinction between vibe coding and agentic coding

Vibe coding with Claude (Anthropic), accessed via the Claude for VS Code extension and the claude.ai web interface; model and extension versions not stated. Proposed: Minimum Viability Framework for Vibe-Coded Applications (security, code quality, accountability layers). Baseline: classical manual development (estimated, not executed)

Vibe coding: none beyond natural-language prompts (e.g. 'Create a React Task Manager application with ...'). Framework: OWASP ZAP/Snyk scan with all High/Medium findings resolved; reviewed ESLint pass; basic test suite (authentication and CRUD, e.g. Jest); SonarQube; developer sign-off on the full codebase

Vibe coding loop: prompt -> AI generates code -> user copies into VS Code -> runs app -> visual check in browser -> refinement prompt (Fig. 2). Framework: three sequential pre-deployment layers: (1) security vulnerability baseline, (2) code quality/maintainability, (3) human ownership/accountability

Vibe coding: only visual confirmation in the browser after each iteration (no code review). Framework: mandatory post-generation review before deployment: resolve High/Medium scan findings, developer review of lint output, and a developer who can read, explain and sign off on the codebase
Vibe coding workflow run end to end; the proposed framework is not run (document-based)
Not classifiable (vibe coding without specifications; authors contrast vibe coding with agentic coding)
New project (greenfield Task Manager CRUD web app) plus one feature extension (dashboard module)
One application, about 18 files and 1,200 lines of code (JS/JSX); 7 development stages plus 1 extension with 3 activities
Web application: task management (CRUD, authentication, priority filtering, real-time search, dashboard); stack chosen by the AI: React, Node.js 20+ with Express, JSON/localStorage
One developer (experience Not stated) doing the vibe coding; three developers with 2-5 years full-stack experience gave the classical-development estimates

Implementation time per stage (minutes), from first prompt to functionality visibly operational in the browser without blocking errors, including model wait, copy and run, excluding user reflection pauses; average of three runs. No tokens or money
Visual confirmation that each functionality is operational in the browser without blocking errors; no tests
ESLint v8 (Airbnb config) warnings and errors; code duplication; test coverage; architectural separation (MVC), by manual review; remediation effort rated per dimension
Prompting iterations per feature (average 2-3); estimated classical development time per stage by three developers
Security vulnerabilities by OWASP category and severity (OWASP ZAP active scan); error categories during generation (logical, integration, syntax/runtime)

Direct timing averaged over three runs; classical times from literature data cross-validated with independent estimates of three developers (ranges); OWASP ZAP active scan on the locally deployed app; ESLint v8 static analysis; manual structural review

Task Manager case study. Vibe coding + Claude (VS Code extension / claude.ai, model version not stated): total 43 min for 7 stages (setup 3, UI 5, CRUD 8, filtering/search 4, auth 6, styling 5, debugging 12; mean of 3 runs); dashboard extension 8 min; 2-3 prompt iterations per feature; interface difference negligible. Security: 5 OWASP categories — A01 missing authentication on API routes (High), A02 plaintext passwords (High), A03 XSS (Medium), A07 no rate limiting (Medium), A05 missing security headers (Low). Code quality: 47 ESLint warnings, 12 errors; duplicated error handling; 0% test coverage; partial MVC separation. Authors' criteria: functionality visibly operational (met) and their Minimum Viability Framework baseline (all High/Medium findings resolved, tests present: not met). Quality verdict: partly (functional per the authors' check, fails their security and quality baseline); cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. Classical development (baseline, estimated only): 340-495 min; dashboard 100-140 min — quality and cost verdicts: N/A (not executed)
fields.why: Values match Tables I-IV. The only success check used during the run is 'visibly operational in the browser without blocking errors' (p. 3); the security/quality baseline (Table V) is proposed afterwards, though the authors state the app 'does not meet the baseline quality standards' (p. 6) and its security 'would be unacceptable in any production context' (p. 8). 'Partly' combines both; 'does not work' (production) or 'works' (prototype) are also defensible.
fields.doubt: O único critério durante a execução é a app funcionar no browser; o baseline de segurança e qualidade (Tabela V) é proposto depois. Decide se o veredicto de qualidade é partly, does not work ou works (protótipo).

fields.v: One application and one feature extension; vibe coding by one developer with Claude vs classical development estimated from literature and three developers (not executed); same feature list; testing, documentation, security auditing and refactoring excluded from both; vibe-coding times averaged over three runs; stack chosen freely by the AI; no acceptance tests (visual check); human intervention: user writes prompts, copies code and verifies, no manual code

Vibe coding 43 min vs classical 340-495 min (~88% reduction); dashboard 8 vs 100-140 min (~14x faster). No statistical test. Authors stress this is time-to-first-working-demo and does not establish quality equivalence; the vibe-coded app had 2 High and 2 Medium vulnerabilities and no tests

Showed a large time difference, but against an estimated baseline. Limitations stated by the authors: classical times are practitioner estimates, not measurements; reflection pauses excluded (underestimates effort for inexperienced users); estimate ranges do not cover junior to senior; only time-to-demo; no standardised benchmark for vibe coding efficiency; replication not guaranteed since the AI chooses the stack

Limitations: single developer, model, stack and application; illustrative, not generalisable; estimated baseline; exclusions from timing; stack variability between sessions/models; debugging did not always converge, especially for integration failures. Gaps/future work: longitudinal maintainability of vibe-coded applications; automated auditing pipelines for AI-generated code; effects on technical skill development in professional and educational contexts

No replication package (only example prompts); no pre-registration. Language: JavaScript/JSX (React, Node.js/Express). Model version not stated ('Claude'; chosen over GPT-4 and Gemini). Inconsistencies: dashboard classical effort given as 90-120 min in the text vs 100-140 min in Table II (p. 4); ESLint counts reported 'across the React front-end' although the pass covered front-end and back-end (p. 5); localStorage tokens without expiration reported in the Discussion but not in Table III (pp. 5-6); ~88% reduction is approximate (87-91% from Table I). Code was copied manually from chat, so the agent did not operate on files itself
